**Interpret obligations by role and date.** Before assuming a requirement applies, identify whether the system is covered, which actor has the obligation, whether the relevant provision has become applicable and whether a transitional rule changes the position. For a high-risk admissions system, provider obligations concerning design and documentation differ from deployer obligations concerning operational use and oversight. A university may need to coordinate these with GDPR assessments and procurement documentation without treating the instruments as interchangeable.
lessons.example: A vendor markets a tool that ranks admissions applicants. A second tool only formats text without influencing selection. Compare the intended purposes, possible Article 6(3) conditions, profiling, human oversight and the date on which the relevant high-risk provisions apply.
lessons.nuance: High-risk does not mean prohibited. Classification depends on intended purpose and the applicable legal conditions. Dates should be rechecked before practical reliance.

questions.statement: Every AI tool used at a university is high-risk solely because its user is a university.
questions.explanation: The specific intended purpose and Article 6 classification criteria matter.

questions.statement: An Annex III admissions system can be high-risk even though its vendor is not a university.
questions.explanation: The intended admissions use, not the vendor’s institutional identity, drives classification.

questions.statement: The general Annex III high-risk application date is 2 December 2027 under the July 2026 amendments.
questions.explanation: The amendment extends this deadline; other duties may already apply.

questions.statement: Article 6(3) can exempt certain Annex III systems only if its conditions are met.
questions.explanation: The exception is conditional and profiling excludes its use.

questions.statement: An AI Act fundamental rights impact assessment automatically replaces a required GDPR DPIA.
questions.explanation: The assessments have distinct legal bases and can complement one another.

questions.statement: The delayed high-risk application date does not suspend GDPR requirements for AI processing.
questions.explanation: The AI Act does not displace applicable data protection law.

questions.statement: A system that profiles natural persons cannot use the Article 6(3) exception for Annex III systems.
questions.explanation: Article 6(3) expressly treats such profiling systems as high-risk.

questions.statement: An application date for Annex III systems establishes the same application date for all prohibited practices.
questions.explanation: The AI Act has distinct dates for its different provisions.

lessons.title: Participation consent and research lawful bases
lessons.objective: Separate informed consent from the GDPR basis.
concepts: Agreement to participate in research and GDPR consent serve different purposes. A study can rely on another valid Article 6 basis while obtaining ethical participation consent.
GDPR consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent.
For special categories, an Article 9 condition is also necessary. Dutch UAVG Article 24 provides a conditional research exception.

**Two decisions for participants.** Informed consent to take part protects autonomy in the study. GDPR consent authorizes processing if it is the chosen basis. A participant can discontinue participation even where certain lawfully collected data remain subject to another valid basis or retention requirement; explain the actual limits in advance.

**Special categories in Dutch research.** Article 9(2)(j) and Article 89(1) must be read with applicable national law. UAVG Article 24 sets cumulative conditions, including necessity for research/statistics, public interest, impossibility or disproportionate effort of obtaining explicit consent, and safeguards. Do not assume the exception simply because an ethics committee approved the study.

**Recruitment and dependency.** A lecturer recruiting their own students or a supervisor recruiting employees must consider voluntariness and possible detriment. Independent recruitment, equivalent alternatives and clear separation of assessment from participation can reduce pressure. Document the legal basis separately from the ethical process.

**Explain the actual choice.** Participant information should distinguish ethical consent, the legal basis for processing, what happens when participation stops, what information may remain and why, and who can receive data. When reliance on consent is proposed, examine whether consent can be free in the recruitment relationship. When reliance on a research exception is proposed, check its actual Dutch legal conditions. An ethics committee can assess participant protection, but its decision does not remove the controller's responsibility for processing.
lessons.example: A cognitive experiment involves students who can choose an alternative course activity. It collects information about diagnosed learning disabilities. The team must separately address participation consent, Article 6, Article 9, Dutch law, access and safeguards. An ethics approval is relevant to research governance but does not establish those legal conditions.
lessons.nuance: Recital 33 recognizes that some scientific research purposes cannot be fully identified initially, but it does not authorize unlimited consent.

questions.statement: A signed research participation form establishes GDPR consent for every later use of the data.
questions.explanation: GDPR consent has its own conditions and scope. Later purposes require separate consideration.

questions.statement: Ethical participation consent can coexist with a different GDPR lawful basis.
questions.explanation: The two concepts are distinct; the chosen GDPR basis must satisfy Article 6.

questions.statement: Scientific research automatically permits processing special-category data under Dutch law.
questions.explanation: Article 9 and UAVG Article 24 impose conditions; research status alone is not enough.

questions.statement: Ethics committee approval itself constitutes an Article 6 lawful basis.
questions.explanation: Ethics approval is not one of the six bases.

questions.statement: A Dutch research exception for special categories has conditions beyond scientific purpose.
questions.explanation: UAVG Article 24 contains cumulative conditions.

questions.statement: The consequences of withdrawal from participation can differ from withdrawal of GDPR consent.
questions.explanation: The ethical participation decision and the Article 7 legal basis are distinct.

questions.statement: A researcher can ethically ask a participant to stop or decline a study activity without making GDPR consent the legal basis.
questions.explanation: Ethical participation and the GDPR lawful basis are separate decisions.

questions.statement: A research exception based on Article 9(2)(j) eliminates the requirement to minimize access to health records.
questions.explanation: Article 89 safeguards and the Article 5 principles remain applicable.

lessons.title: Secondary use, retention and research safeguards
lessons.objective: Understand compatibility and research-specific safeguards.
concepts: Further processing for scientific research is not considered incompatible with the initial purposes under Article 5(1)(b) when Article 89(1) applies.
Longer storage for research can be permitted subject to appropriate safeguards; GDPR itself sets no universal ten-year research retention period.
Article 89 requires safeguards, especially minimization. UAVG Article 44 allows certain rights to be limited in specified research/statistical circumstances.

**Compatibility is only one part of reuse.** The research rule in Article 5(1)(b) is linked to Article 89. Check whether the original legal basis can support further processing, whether the recipient has its own lawful basis and whether special-category conditions apply. New disclosure is itself a processing operation.

**Safeguards follow the dataset and purpose.** Consider pseudonymization, separation of keys, restricted access, confidentiality, data-use limitations and publication risk. Where research can be achieved without identifying people, Article 89(1) favors that approach. Open science does not require public release of identifiable records.

**Rights and retention.** Article 89 permits defined derogations only under conditions and applicable law. UAVG Article 44 concerns specific rights in scientific or statistical contexts; it does not abolish all rights. Distinguish institutional research integrity retention from GDPR rules, and justify identifiable retention separately from retention of anonymous results.

**Controlled access is a substantive safeguard.** If the research value requires detailed records, evaluate whether controlled access with a data-use agreement, restricted workspace, limited output review and prohibition of re-identification can reduce disclosure risk. These are possible measures, not automatic proof of compliance. The recipient's role, purpose, legal basis, transfer status and security still matter. If research can be conducted without identifying people, Article 89 points toward that approach. A promise of open science should not be read as a promise of unrestricted release of personal data.
lessons.example: An archive contains consent forms, raw audio, coded transcripts and final aggregate statistics. A new research team wants the coded data for secondary analysis. Compare controlled access, anonymous release and unrestricted publication, taking account of the original participant information and the possibility of indirect identification.
lessons.nuance: Open science does not require public release of personal data. Institutional retention rules and funder requirements must be considered separately.

questions.statement: GDPR itself imposes a ten-year minimum retention period on all university research data.
questions.explanation: Retention depends on purpose, applicable law and safeguards; institutional requirements are separate.

questions.statement: Research compatibility under Article 5(1)(b) is linked to Article 89(1) safeguards.
questions.explanation: The special compatibility rule expressly refers to Article 89(1).

questions.statement: UAVG Article 44 removes all data subject rights for any research activity.
questions.explanation: It addresses specific rights and conditions, not a blanket exemption.

questions.statement: Article 89 safeguards can include pseudonymization when appropriate.
questions.explanation: Article 89(1) specifically identifies this as a possible measure.

questions.statement: An open-science policy automatically permits public disclosure of identifiable interview transcripts.
questions.explanation: Disclosure remains subject to lawfulness, purpose limitation and safeguards.

questions.statement: A new recipient acting as independent controller must assess its own lawful basis.
questions.explanation: Each controller is responsible for the processing it determines.

questions.statement: The research storage exception can support indefinite operational access to identifiable records merely because a future study is imaginable.
questions.explanation: Extended retention must meet the specified research purpose and safeguards, not speculative operational use.

questions.statement: Article 89(1) favors processing that does not permit identification where the research purpose can be achieved that way.
questions.explanation: The provision requires that approach when feasible for the purpose.

lessons.title: International collaborations and AI development
lessons.objective: Distinguish sharing arrangements, transfers and research exclusions.
concepts: Partners’ controller/processor roles depend on actual purposes and means. Sharing personal data must have a lawful basis and appropriate safeguards.
Chapter V applies to qualifying transfers to third countries or international organizations. Adequacy, appropriate safeguards or narrowly applicable derogations are different routes.
Research-only AI exclusions are purpose-dependent. A research system later deployed in student services must be reassessed.

**When Chapter V applies.** EDPB Guidelines 05/2021 explain the distinction between GDPR territorial scope and transfers. A GDPR-subject exporter making data available to a distinct importer in a third country can trigger Chapter V even where the importer is itself subject to GDPR. Remote access by a separate overseas recipient may count; location alone is not the whole analysis.

**Transfer mechanisms.** Check the scope of any adequacy decision. Otherwise Article 46 mechanisms such as appropriate standard contractual clauses may apply; assess third-country law and supplementary measures where necessary. Article 49 derogations are limited and not a general replacement for regular transfer arrangements.

**AI research collaboration.** Identify whether partners receive raw training data, coded records, model weights, outputs or anonymous statistics. Models and outputs can present disclosure or inference risks. An agreement should accurately reflect roles, data access, transfer routes, security, retention and any intended secondary use.

**Follow the data flow, not the country label.** Record who exports, who receives, how they gain access, the processing purpose and applicable transfer route. An EU-based collaborator traveling abroad within the same organization is not necessarily a separate importer; this is distinct from making records available to a separate foreign partner. Both situations can require security assessment. A vendor's statement that its service is European-hosted does not answer all recipient and access questions. Check actual organizational entities, contractual roles and legal safeguards.
lessons.example: A Dutch university and a non-EEA partner jointly study identifiable speech recordings. The partner accesses recordings on an EU-hosted server. Consider the separate recipient and remote access, whether an appropriate transfer mechanism is available, and whether a less revealing data representation could meet the research purpose.
lessons.nuance: Access from abroad may be relevant even without downloading. A collaboration agreement alone is not a Chapter V transfer mechanism.

questions.statement: A collaboration agreement alone establishes a valid GDPR transfer mechanism for all third-country recipients.
questions.explanation: Chapter V requires an applicable mechanism and conditions; an ordinary collaboration agreement is not sufficient.

questions.statement: A research-only AI system later used operationally should be reassessed under the AI Act.
questions.explanation: The scope exclusion depends on the system’s scientific-only purpose and use.

questions.statement: Adequacy decisions must be checked for their scope, rather than assuming they cover every recipient in a country.
questions.explanation: Adequacy can apply to a country, territory, specified sector or international organization.

questions.statement: EU server hosting alone rules out a third-country transfer to a separate overseas recipient.
questions.explanation: Making data available to a separate importer abroad can trigger Chapter V.

questions.statement: An importer can be subject to GDPR and still receive data in a Chapter V transfer.
questions.explanation: Territorial scope and transfer rules are distinct.

questions.statement: Article 49 derogations provide a general default for recurring research transfers.
questions.explanation: They have specific conditions and limited scope.

questions.statement: Remote access by a separate foreign research partner can constitute making data available to an importer.
questions.explanation: EDPB transfer guidance includes making data accessible to a distinct third-country recipient.

questions.statement: A transfer mechanism removes the need to identify an Article 6 lawful basis for disclosure.
questions.explanation: Chapter V and the general lawfulness requirements are cumulative.

lessons.title: Student records, examinations and retention
lessons.objective: Connect GDPR principles with Dutch education responsibilities.
concepts: Student administration and examination processing require a specific purpose, lawful basis, access controls and defined retention.
WHW Articles 7.12 and 7.12b establish the examination board and its responsibilities. This does not grant unrestricted access to every student record.
Erasure requests must be assessed against relevant legal obligations and other exceptions, rather than handled automatically.

**Distinguish educational records.** Enrollment information, formal grade decisions, examination scripts, misconduct allegations, accommodation information and platform logs have different purposes and sensitivity. Define which legal task or duty supports each processing operation, and restrict access accordingly.

**Examination governance.** The WHW assigns responsibilities to examination boards. That does not grant blanket access to all information held about students. The board may need evidence relevant to a decision, while a teacher or administrator needs a different subset. Consider the distinction between formal decisions and working materials.

**Retention and rights.** Identify statutory requirements, applicable institutional retention rules, appeal procedures and the necessity of retaining particular categories. A student request for erasure or access must be evaluated under GDPR, including relevant exceptions and other individuals' rights.

**Separate academic governance from data protection.** The examination board may need to evaluate whether a decision meets the applicable examination rules. The controller must also determine lawful access, transparency, security, retention and rights for personal data involved. A student's request may combine a challenge to a grade with a request for a copy of personal data. Route each element appropriately rather than rejecting one because the other is already being addressed. Consider third-party information and the specific statutory or institutional retention schedule.
lessons.example: A student challenges a grade and requests access to their exam and related records. The university holds their submitted answers, the examiner's notes, other students' results and an internal decision record. Consider which material contains the student's personal data, whether other people's data need protection, and how the academic appeal differs from GDPR rights.
lessons.nuance: Retention periods for exam scripts may depend on institutional schedules and other rules. Do not infer a single period from GDPR or WHW.

questions.statement: The examination board’s statutory duties permit it to see every student’s health information without a necessity assessment.
questions.explanation: Access must still be justified and minimized; health data have extra protection.

questions.statement: A student’s erasure request can be limited by an applicable statutory retention obligation.
questions.explanation: Article 17(3)(b) may apply where processing is necessary to comply with a legal obligation.

questions.statement: The examination board has a statutory role in determining whether degree requirements are met.
questions.explanation: This follows from WHW Article 7.12(2).

questions.statement: Examination records and platform activity logs can require different retention assessments.
questions.explanation: Purpose and necessity are category-specific.

questions.statement: An examination board's role automatically authorizes disclosure of unrelated medical details to all lecturers.
questions.explanation: Access must be necessary for the purpose and special-category conditions must be satisfied.

questions.statement: An academic appeal and a GDPR access request are legally distinct procedures.
questions.explanation: Academic review and Article 15 rights have different purposes.

questions.statement: An examination board can receive only the student data relevant and necessary for its assigned decision, even if additional data are easily available.
questions.explanation: Data minimization applies to access and use in the specific task.

questions.statement: A grade appeal automatically removes the student's GDPR access rights for the associated personal data.
questions.explanation: The appeal and GDPR rights are distinct; applicable limitations need their own assessment.

lessons.title: Learning analytics, proctoring and accommodations
lessons.objective: Assess monitoring and sensitive student data.
concepts: Learning analytics and remote proctoring can involve profiling or systematic monitoring. A DPIA may be required where high risk is likely.
Information about disability or health is special-category data. An applicable Article 9 condition is required; access must be minimized.
AI intended to detect prohibited behavior during tests is listed in Annex III(3)(d); Article 6 classification and the updated implementation calendar matter.

**Monitoring and inference.** Learning analytics may transform ordinary log data into behavioral predictions. Examine whether the inference relates to an individual, how reliable it is, who receives it and whether it affects grades or access to support. False signals and chilling effects are relevant privacy harms.

**Proctoring.** Consider the purpose, necessity, less intrusive exam designs, extent of recording, retention, access and impact on the home environment. A mandatory checkbox is not automatically free consent. High-risk processing may require a DPIA under GDPR independently of the AI Act timetable.

**Accommodations.** Health information is subject to Article 9. Staff may need to know the adjustment (such as extra time) rather than the diagnosis. Identify the applicable legal condition, including Dutch provisions when relevant, and avoid unnecessary disclosure.

**Evaluate impact beyond privacy notices.** A learning analytics system might create an inaccurate prediction that changes how teachers treat an individual. Consider whether learners can understand and challenge the inference, whether data are accurate for the intended purpose, whether the system uses sensitive proxies and whether a less intrusive support mechanism exists. If accommodation information is needed, restrict who can see it. A DPIA can bring these questions together but cannot substitute for a lawful basis.
lessons.example: A proctoring tool flags frequent eye movement as potential misconduct. Students with certain disabilities may be disproportionately flagged. Compare automated flagging with an examiner's contextual evaluation and alternative exam arrangements. Distinguish technical performance, necessity, fairness and the legal effect of any final decision.
lessons.nuance: Consent may be difficult to establish as freely given when students lack a genuine choice. Assess alternatives rather than assuming consent resolves monitoring risks.

questions.statement: Student disability information can constitute special-category health data.
questions.explanation: Information revealing physical or mental health is covered by Article 9.

questions.statement: A mandatory proctoring checkbox necessarily establishes freely given GDPR consent.
questions.explanation: A lack of real choice can undermine consent.

questions.statement: AI intended to monitor prohibited behavior during examinations is explicitly listed in Annex III.
questions.explanation: Annex III(3)(d) lists this use; Article 6 and transition dates still matter.

questions.statement: An instructor may need accommodation instructions without needing the underlying medical diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Minimization requires limiting data to what the purpose needs.

questions.statement: A proctoring system's high detection accuracy by itself establishes proportionality.
questions.explanation: Necessity, alternatives and impact on individuals still matter.

questions.statement: GDPR DPIA requirements can apply before AI Act high-risk obligations become applicable.
questions.explanation: The statutes have separate triggers and dates.

questions.statement: A student can be affected by an inaccurate learning analytics inference even when the original activity log is correct.
questions.explanation: Derived personal data must be evaluated for accuracy and fairness in relation to their purpose.

questions.statement: Completing a DPIA makes a monitoring activity lawful even if no valid Article 6 basis has been identified.
questions.explanation: Risk assessment does not establish a lawful basis.

lessons.title: AI-assisted admissions and grading
lessons.objective: Distinguish high-risk AI classification, human review and automated decisions.
concepts: AI intended to determine access/admission or evaluate learning outcomes can be listed high-risk under Annex III(3), subject to Article 6.
GDPR Article 22 applies to solely automated significant decisions, with specific exceptions and safeguards. A human rubber stamp may not amount to genuine human involvement.
AI Act human oversight and GDPR automated-decision rules are separate requirements. High-risk application deadlines do not postpone GDPR.

**Assess the actual decision.** Identify whether AI produces advice, an intermediate score or a final outcome. Under GDPR Article 22, solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects are subject to special restrictions and exceptions. Genuine human involvement requires actual authority and the ability to evaluate and change the outcome.

**Case law.** SCHUFA (C-634/21) demonstrates that an intermediate automated score can fall within Article 22 if it determines the subsequent decision in practice. The label 'recommendation' is not decisive. In education, assess how the examiner or admissions officer actually uses the result.

**High-risk classification is different.** Annex III(3) lists specified systems for educational access, learning outcomes, educational level and examination monitoring. Human review may reduce risks without automatically removing the system from Annex III. Check Article 6 and the amended dates.

**Human review as a real process.** Evaluate whether the reviewer receives sufficient information, can identify errors, has authority to disregard the recommendation, has adequate time and records independent reasoning. A policy saying that humans remain responsible is not enough if decisions are effectively automatic. Where Article 22 exceptions apply, additional safeguards may be necessary. High-risk AI obligations have their own triggers and dates; a university should design oversight and procurement with both regimes in mind.
lessons.example: A faculty uses an automated model to recommend admission decisions. Officers see scores but lack time or information to challenge them and almost always accept them. Compare a process where a trained officer independently assesses the evidence and can meaningfully change the recommendation. GDPR and AI Act assessments remain separate.
lessons.nuance: Human review can matter for Article 22 but does not automatically remove an AI system from Annex III classification.

questions.statement: Adding an examiner’s approval button automatically makes the decision non-automated under GDPR.
questions.explanation: Actual meaningful involvement matters, not a nominal approval step.

questions.statement: An AI system evaluating learning outcomes can fall within Annex III even when an examiner reviews its output.
questions.explanation: Human review does not itself settle Article 6 classification.

questions.statement: The delayed AI Act high-risk deadline suspends GDPR Article 22 for university grading.
questions.explanation: GDPR applies independently.

questions.statement: An intermediate AI score can be relevant to Article 22 if it determines the final decision in practice.
questions.explanation: The SCHUFA judgment recognizes this possibility.

questions.statement: Meaningful human oversight is established solely by giving a staff member an approval button.
questions.explanation: Actual ability and authority to assess and change the outcome matter.

questions.statement: A human-reviewed learning-outcome system can still fall within Annex III.
questions.explanation: The listing and Article 6 conditions apply independently of human review.

questions.statement: An admissions officer's actual authority to reject an AI recommendation is relevant to assessing meaningful human involvement.
questions.explanation: The practical role of the human decision-maker matters to whether the decision is solely automated.

questions.statement: An AI system used to evaluate learning outcomes becomes outside Annex III solely because its output is described as advisory.
questions.explanation: Intended purpose and Article 6 conditions determine classification, not the label alone.

lessons.title: Procurement, cloud services and subprocessors
lessons.objective: Recognize controller duties and processor chains.
concepts: A processor contract must include Article 28 requirements, including instructions, confidentiality, security, assistance and return/deletion provisions.
A processor needs specific or general written authorization before engaging another processor. General authorization requires notice of intended changes and opportunity to object.
Where a supplier uses data for its own purposes, its role for that activity must be assessed separately.

**Procurement starts with processing facts.** Identify data types, purposes, actual roles, hosting, remote support, subcontractors and deletion arrangements. Check whether the vendor uses inputs for its own training or product improvement. A contract label does not override actual activities.

**Article 28 contract contents.** Specify subject matter, duration, nature and purposes, data types, categories of people, instructions and applicable obligations. Check confidentiality, security, assistance with rights and breaches, audits, subprocessor authorization and end-of-service return or deletion. Subprocessor obligations must flow down.

**Verify changes.** Under general written authorization, the processor informs the controller of intended additions or replacements and allows objections. Determine whether new remote access or onward transfers require additional safeguards. Avoid signing redundant contracts when a valid arrangement already covers the actual processing, but reassess material changes.

**Distinguish contract assurance from evidence.** Read the supplier's instructions and rights obligations alongside security architecture, retention settings, subprocessor list, service changes and remote access arrangements. If a vendor is both processor and controller for distinct activities, document those activities separately. Check whether contract clauses actually cover the new AI features or whether an amendment and reassessment are necessary. The objective is an accurate and enforceable arrangement rather than merely obtaining another signed agreement.
lessons.example: A university procures cloud transcription. The vendor stores recordings in Europe, uses an overseas support firm and proposes using recordings to train its own model. Analyze hosting, remote support and model training separately. A processor agreement may cover transcription but cannot simply authorize the vendor's independent purpose as instructed processing.
lessons.nuance: An EU server location is not proof that all processing, support or transfers stay within the EEA.

references.location: Remote access and separate importer criteria

questions.statement: A processor can engage a subprocessor without any written authorization if it remains responsible for the service.
questions.explanation: Article 28(2) requires specific or general written authorization.

questions.statement: Under general authorization, intended subprocessor changes must be communicated so the controller can object.
questions.explanation: Article 28(2) explicitly requires this opportunity.

questions.statement: An EU hosting address establishes that every remote support activity remains in the EEA.
questions.explanation: Access arrangements and actual recipients must be checked separately.

questions.statement: A processor must assist with data subject rights as required under Article 28.
questions.explanation: Article 28(3)(e) requires appropriate assistance.

questions.statement: A processor can retain all personal data for its own unrelated model training merely because it has a DPA.
questions.explanation: Own-purpose processing needs a separate role and lawfulness assessment.

questions.statement: Article 28 requires arrangements for return or deletion at the end of service, subject to applicable legal retention.
questions.explanation: Article 28(3)(g) addresses this.

questions.statement: Under specific written authorization, adding a new subprocessor requires the applicable controller authorization.
questions.explanation: Article 28(2) requires prior specific or general written authorization; specific authorization is not blanket permission.

questions.statement: The existence of a processor agreement makes the processor's own unrelated data use part of the controller's instructions.
questions.explanation: Independent purposes must be assessed on their own facts; Article 28(10) addresses role changes.

lessons.title: Staff monitoring, recruitment and health data
lessons.objective: Apply GDPR and AI Act concepts to employment.
concepts: Employee data processing requires a lawful basis and proportionality. Employment power imbalance can undermine freely given consent.
Health and absence-related data may be special-category data; Dutch law contains limited exceptions. Do not infer unrestricted employer access.
AI for recruitment, selection or specified worker-management decisions is listed in Annex III(4); workplace emotion inference is generally prohibited subject to the medical/safety exception.

**Employment context.** Separate payroll, workplace safety, absence management, recruitment and monitoring. The legal basis depends on the purpose. Employment dependency may make consent unsuitable where refusal is not genuinely possible. A contract is not permission for unrelated tracking.

**Health data.** Employers need to distinguish necessary absence administration from medical diagnosis and treatment. Applicable Dutch rules restrict processing of health data; involve occupational health professionals where appropriate. UAVG Article 30 contains specific health-data exceptions, not unrestricted permission.

**AI employment systems.** Annex III(4) covers specified recruitment and worker-management uses, subject to Article 6. Biometric emotion inference at work is generally prohibited subject to the specified medical or safety exceptions. Dutch employment and participation rules can also be relevant; check the applicable process separately.

**Necessity and fairness in employee monitoring.** Distinguish measuring service delivery at team level from continuous individualized surveillance. Evaluate less intrusive alternatives, the sensitivity of the information, reasonable employee expectations, retention, access and the consequences of errors. A tool used for performance evaluation or promotion may raise both GDPR and AI Act questions. Dutch participation and employment rules can also require separate attention. A measure suitable for payroll administration is not necessarily appropriate for monitoring productivity.
lessons.example: A department proposes monitoring keystrokes to assess employee productivity and using an AI model to rank staff for promotion. Consider whether less intrusive evidence meets the purpose, the legal basis, fairness, transparency, the need for a DPIA and the AI Act classification. Distinguish the monitoring from ordinary payroll administration.
lessons.nuance: High-risk obligations apply according to the updated calendar, while prohibited practices and GDPR already apply.

questions.statement: An employment contract makes any form of employee monitoring necessary for contract performance.
questions.explanation: Necessity and proportionality must be established for the specific processing.

questions.statement: AI intended to rank job applicants can be listed high-risk under the AI Act.
questions.explanation: Recruitment and selection are included in Annex III(4)(a).

questions.statement: An employer’s legitimate interest alone is enough to process special-category health data.
questions.explanation: An applicable Article 9 condition is also required.

questions.statement: An employer may have a valid payroll basis without thereby having a basis for continuous productivity monitoring.
questions.explanation: Different purposes require their own necessity and lawfulness assessment.

questions.statement: A staff member's signed consent automatically removes the employment power imbalance.
questions.explanation: The actual conditions determine whether consent is freely given.

questions.statement: AI intended for specified decisions about worker promotion can fall within Annex III(4).
questions.explanation: Worker management uses are included in the annex, subject to classification rules.

questions.statement: Team-level statistics that do not identify individual workers may be a less intrusive alternative to personal monitoring.
questions.explanation: An effective non-identifying alternative is relevant to necessity and minimization.

questions.statement: An AI provider's claim of high accuracy alone establishes that a university may lawfully rank staff for promotion.
questions.explanation: Lawfulness, necessity, fairness and applicable AI Act requirements must still be examined.

lessons.title: Breaches, responsibilities and oversight
lessons.objective: Distinguish institutional accountability from specialist duties.
concepts: A personal data breach can concern confidentiality, integrity or availability. Controllers document breaches and notify the authority unless risk to individuals is unlikely.
Where notification is required, the controller must notify without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after awareness. Processors notify controllers without undue delay.
The DPO advises and monitors independently. The controller remains accountable. A high-risk breach may also require communication to affected individuals.

**A breach is not just a cyberattack.** Misdirected emails, accidental deletion and unauthorized alteration can be breaches. Identify what happened, data categories, affected people, recipients, containment and potential consequences. Document facts and decisions even when authority notification is not required.

**Two thresholds.** Notify the supervisory authority unless a risk to individuals is unlikely; communicate to affected people when high risk is likely, subject to Article 34 exceptions. These are different thresholds. The controller should act without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after awareness for required authority notification; explain any delay.

**Responsibilities.** A processor informs the controller without undue delay after awareness. A DPO advises and monitors; the controller remains accountable. Internal staff should use the institutional reporting route promptly and not make unilateral legal notification decisions outside their assigned responsibilities.

**Incident decision-making exercise.** First contain the incident, preserve relevant facts and notify the responsible institutional team. Then establish whether personal data were involved, what type of breach occurred, the likely consequences and whether the Article 33 and 34 thresholds are met. Notification can be phased where full information is not available at once, as Article 33(4) allows. Record what was known at each point, the measures taken and the rationale for the decision. Do not wait for perfect certainty before escalation.
lessons.example: A staff member emails a spreadsheet with sensitive student accommodation details to an unintended external recipient. Contain the incident, assess whether the recipient accessed or deleted the file, identify affected people and possible consequences, and document the reasoning for notification and communication. A recipient's assurance is relevant but not automatically decisive.
lessons.nuance: Not every security incident is a personal data breach, and not every breach requires notification. Internal reporting deadlines can be stricter.

questions.statement: A controller must document personal data breaches even when notification to the authority is not required.
questions.explanation: Article 33(5) requires documentation of breaches and relevant facts.

questions.statement: A processor has the same 72-hour statutory notification deadline to the authority as a controller.
questions.explanation: The processor must notify the controller without undue delay; the controller assesses authority notification.

questions.statement: Appointing a DPO transfers the controller’s responsibility for compliance to the DPO.
questions.explanation: The DPO advises and monitors; accountability remains with the controller.

questions.statement: Authority notification and communication to individuals have different risk thresholds.
questions.explanation: Articles 33 and 34 apply risk and high-risk tests respectively.

questions.statement: A breach involving accidental alteration is outside the personal data breach definition.
questions.explanation: The definition includes accidental or unlawful alteration.

questions.statement: A notification made after 72 hours must include reasons for the delay where notification is required.
questions.explanation: Article 33(1) expressly requires reasons when notification is not made within 72 hours.

questions.statement: A required breach notification may provide information in phases when it cannot all be provided at the same time.
questions.explanation: Article 33(4) allows phased provision without undue further delay.

questions.statement: A controller must communicate every notified breach to all affected individuals regardless of the risk level.
questions.explanation: Article 34 uses a high-risk threshold and specified exceptions, distinct from Article 33.
